rv.q: You can forgive this contrivance because the humour and zesty dialogue in this play is so cleverly barbed.
Cromwell’s production has a hectic energy designed to carry us over the flaws.
The three actors do their very best to keep The Authenticator on course, but in the end it's a lost cause.
But perhaps because it’s all played so lightly, it’s unclear what it’s looking to say.
There’s much to enjoy in this production, but it needs to be more focused to authenticate its own identity.
It is complex, compelling and quietly devastating.
While it might not be completely perfect, there is more than enough on offer here to authenticate its quality in a truly impressive production.
With inventive staging, strong performances, and an engaging plot, it’s a compelling addition to the National Theatre’s current season.
And yet, it is this awkward juxtaposition that becomes The Authenticator’s true strength.
But as a tense, talky, quietly incendiary three-hander about race, legacy and intellectual power, it cuts deeper than any jump scare.
It’s rather unsatisfying, then, for theatregoers looking to be startled.
But it feels oddly lazy for the NT: as if any play about the disgrace and misery of the slave trade gets a free pass, exempt from any rigour in playbuilding, character and probability.
But whenever the play works up a head of steam, it lets itself down.
